synthesis.headline: South Texas cutoff low winds down as the ridge shifts to central Canada and an eastern storm looms
synthesis.narrative:
No severe weather is expected anywhere today, and surface highs of 1022 to 1028 mb keep most of the country quiet. The one real hazard is still South Texas. The closed low near the Rio Grande, soaking the region for several days now, is drawing Gulf moisture into elevated storms with locally very heavy downpours. WPC has a Slight Risk of excessive rainfall near the lower Texas coast and the Rio Grande delta, inside a Marginal Risk that reaches into northeastern Mexico. The rain eases by evening, and Tuesday's outlook is blank. A fast trough brings rain, mountain snow and some lightning to coastal Washington and Oregon late today. Weak lows near 1001 mb over southern Quebec and Ontario bring showers to the lower Great Lakes. A 1002 mb low near the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border drags a cold front through the Prairies and northern Plains. After this morning's frost in the Southeast, a warming trend spreads.

At 500 mb the flow is split. A 588 dam high sits over California, Arizona and Baja, and a separate cutoff low of about 576-579 dam sits over South Texas, well east of it. Because the high is not poleward of the low, this is not a Rex block. The westerlies pass far to the cutoff's north, so it will drift and weaken rather than get picked up and carried east. The northern stream is fast and nearly west-to-east, with a jet core above 70 kt over Ontario and Quebec. That fast flow is what amplifies next.

By late week a ridge builds from the southern Plains to central Canada, with Plains highs 10 to 20 degrees above normal. A trough deepens over the East, and a low forming over the Mid-Atlantic Thursday night strengthens offshore Friday. It brings a cold rain, possible early snow on the higher ground of West Virginia and western Pennsylvania, and lake-effect showers. Behind it, highs run 5 to 15 degrees below normal and the first frost or freeze reaches the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys and parts of the Deep South by Saturday. The track is still uncertain. Pacific Northwest rain continues in rounds, and a stronger storm Sunday into Monday reaches northern California and the Sierra. The western ridge of recent days is not coming back. CPC's 6-10 day mean puts the strongest above-normal heights, about 20 dam, near Hudson Bay and the Great Lakes, with below-normal heights off the West Coast. The 8-14 day mean keeps the warm core over the Great Lakes and Ontario. That is a real flip to a western trough and eastern ridge, so the eastern chill should be brief.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong El Niño continues. The Oceanic Niño Index for August-October is +2.46°C, up 0.30 from the prior season, so it is still strengthening, though more slowly. The table carries no issue date. El Niño cool seasons tend to favor an active southern jet stream, and the run of southern-stream lows into Texas fits that tendency, though no single cutoff low can be pinned on it. The hurricane season's final weeks are quiet in the Atlantic, with no development expected for seven days. In the central Pacific, Tropical Storm Pena (40 kt, 1002 mb) is 560 miles south-southwest of Hawaii's South Point. It is moving west and poses no land hazard. Disturbance EP96 has a 10% chance of becoming a tropical cyclone.
synthesis.regional_notes: South Texas: storms are elevated, the low-level atmosphere is only weakly unstable, and the strongest cells should stay offshore through early afternoon. The flood risk is from rainfall rates, not severe storms. Pacific Northwest: the coastal line has 100-300 J/kg of instability and strong winds aloft, but instability is too weak for a meaningful damaging-gust risk. Canada: the Prairie cold front is the sharpest airmass change on the continent this morning. The CPC 6-10 day outlook gives the Dakotas and Minnesota 80-90% odds of above-normal temperatures for November 14-18.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z Monday 9 November analysis shows a fairly weak, high-dominated pattern over the lower 48. The strongest closed highs are about 1028 mb over the northern Rockies/Montana region, with 1025 mb to its south over the Great Basin/Idaho area, and a 1022 mb center over the lower Mississippi Valley and another near 1022 over Texas. A 1017 mb high sits over the western Atlantic off the Southeast coast. None of these is exceptional for November, so they mainly signal broadly quiet, settled conditions rather than a driving feature.

The notable lows are in Canada and the far northern tier: a 1002 mb low near the Saskatchewan/Manitoba border region with a cold front trailing south and west across the northern Plains toward the Dakotas and Montana, and a 1001 mb low near southern Quebec/Ontario, with a frontal system extending southward toward the Great Lakes and Northeast. Deeper lows of 988 to 992 mb appear in the Gulf of Alaska and over the far northeast Atlantic/Labrador Sea, well outside the continental core.

A cold front curves from the Great Lakes southwestward along the Appalachians, running roughly from the Ohio Valley toward the Mid-Atlantic coast, and a separate stationary or weakly defined boundary lies along the mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachians. The front across the northern Plains is the sharper airmass change, with a trough axis (dashed) extending south through the central Plains. Other dashed lines over the Southeast and Gulf Coast mark troughs rather than fronts.

Pressure gradients are tightest in the Pacific Northwest and the far northern tier near the Canadian lows, where isobars crowd and winds are stronger. Across the central and southern US the gradient is slack, with widely spaced isobars and mostly light winds, which fits the cluster of highs there.

The focus for lift is the cold front along the Appalachians and Northeast, plus the northern Plains frontal zone feeding the Canadian low. Gulf moisture appears to be pooling along the Florida and Southeast coast with troughing there, but with high pressure dominant, widespread organized lift looks limited away from the frontal corridors.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis for 00Z on 9 November 2026 is a polar-projection chart, so the upper half of the frame is Arctic Ocean, the Archipelago and Greenland, not the provinces. The dominant feature is a deep 967 hPa low with a tight gradient and a wrapped-up frontal structure on the left side of the chart, over what appears to be the northeast Pacific or Gulf of Alaska sector; the coastline there is hard to read, so its position relative to the continent is uncertain. A second 980 hPa low and a broad 988 hPa low sit to its northwest, and a 1002 hPa high lies between them. Cold fronts trailing from the 967 low sweep south and southeast, and a long boundary extends from near the 995 hPa low in the continental interior south toward the central US.

Over Canada itself, the 995 hPa low sits in the interior, with a cold front curling south through the Prairies toward the northern US and 1021-1024 hPa highs behind it over the western and central US. Farther east, a 990 hPa low with an occluded front lies near the Labrador and Newfoundland sector, trailing a cold front that runs southeast out over the western Atlantic. A separate 1001 hPa low and a front sit over the Great Lakes to Quebec corridor, linking the Canadian pattern to the eastern US.

In the Arctic, a 991 hPa low with an occluded front lies on the west side of Greenland, near Baffin Bay or Davis Strait, flanked by a 1033 hPa high over northern Greenland. Other lows in the high Arctic (983, 988, 994 hPa) sit near the top of the frame, and a 973 hPa low with a front lies on the far right edge, east of Greenland over the Norwegian and Greenland Sea sector. The tightest gradients are around the 967 and 973 hPa lows, the Baffin Bay low, and between the Greenland high and the adjacent lows.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 1200 UTC 9 November 2026 analysis shows a split flow over North America. A closed high sits over the Southwest near the California-Arizona-Baja area, with the 588 dam contour enclosing it, while a closed low is analyzed over south Texas near the Rio Grande, closed by roughly the 576-579 dam contours. The high is located well west of the low, so this is not a Rex block: the anticyclone is neither poleward of the low nor at the same longitude, and the better description is a western ridge with a separate, detached southern-stream cutoff to its east. The Texas low looks genuinely closed off from the westerlies, with weak winds around its core and the main belt of strong flow passing well to the north, so it should behave as a self-retaining feature that drifts or pivots rather than translating quickly downstream.

The main westerlies are carried in a zonal to slightly northwesterly band across the northern tier, with the 552-570 dam contours running from the Pacific Northwest through the northern Plains into the Great Lakes. A jet maximum, shaded in the dark red above 70 kt, sits over the Great Lakes and Ontario-Quebec region, with a broad, elongated yellow and olive wind corridor extending northeastward toward the Northeast and the Canadian Maritimes. A secondary wind maximum of 45-50 kt shows over the northern Rockies and northern Plains, which may indicate a shortwave moving through the northern flow, though the chart does not show a clear trough tilt there.

A closed low is also analyzed over northeastern Canada near the top right of the domain, with heights near 538 dam, and a ridge-like bulge in the contours appears over the northwestern Pacific coast and British Columbia. Across the Gulf and Southeast, flow is weak to moderate westerly with heights near 585-588 dam, which fits the subtropical ridge being strong over the southern tier. Overall the pattern is not progressive in the south, where the cutoff low and Southwest high are quasi-stationary, but the northern stream is fast-moving and zonal enough to remain progressive.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The Air Mass RGB at 1321Z on 9 November shows a strongly contrasting pattern. In the northwest of the domain, over the northern Rockies and northern Plains, a broad swath of blue, purple and white marks cold, dry upper-tropospheric air with extensive high cloud, consistent with a large cold-air trough or cyclonic system just off the left edge of the image. Cloud streams curve northeastward across the Dakotas, Minnesota and the upper Great Lakes, showing the flow turning around the eastern flank of that system.

Across the Northeast, from the lower Great Lakes through New York, New England and the western Atlantic, a broad red-orange area marks dry upper-level air, with embedded cloud bands over southern New England. Its position ahead of the western trough suggests ridging or a post-frontal dry airmass rather than a compact intrusion, so I would call it dry air rather than stratospheric in origin.

The sharpest airmass boundary is a roughly east-west green-to-yellow contrast along about 35N, from northern Texas and Oklahoma across the Mid-South toward the Carolinas and offshore. It is the likely jet corridor, with the tropical-green moist air to the south and the drier, yellower air to the north. Without isotachs, its exact axis cannot be placed.

The main organized convection is a cluster of bright white cloud over eastern Texas and the upper Texas coast, with a second cloud band curving southwest from there over the western Gulf and northeastern Mexico. Another convective cluster sits over the northwestern Caribbean south of Cuba, and cloud streamers appear over southern Mexico and the eastern Pacific. The rest of the Southeast and Gulf of Mexico shows mostly clear green, tropical-moist air with only thin cirrus.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most organized feature in this frame is the extratropical cyclone over the western North Atlantic, with a bright white comma-shaped cloud shield near the right limb and a long cloud band trailing southwest from it, apparently along a cold front. The strongest orange-red and dark purple signatures lie just west of that system and across eastern Canada and Hudson Bay, marking dry, high-PV air wrapping around the cyclonic side of the flow. Further north, a broad purple and magenta region across Canada and the Arctic edge marks the cold, dry polar airmass, and the sharp boundary between it and the green tropical air over the central and eastern US implies a jet corridor running from the Great Lakes toward the Canadian Maritimes. Cloud streaks near the top left, over northwestern Canada, suggest a separate shortwave or low there, though the extreme viewing angle at the limb makes placement uncertain.

Across the tropics, the picture is mostly broad green moist air with scattered convective clusters rather than any well-defined wave. The brightest tropical convection sits over the eastern Pacific south of Mexico and west of Colombia and Ecuador, plus smaller clusters over the northwestern Caribbean near Honduras and Nicaragua. An elongated east-west cloud band stretches across the tropical Atlantic north of Brazil and the Guianas, consistent with an ITCZ-type convergence zone, and several large convective patches dot the Amazon basin. Over the Gulf of Mexico and the western Atlantic off the Southeast US, the green and olive tones with little cloud suggest a quiet, moist but unforced environment.

In the Southern Hemisphere, a strong baroclinic cloud band with a pronounced dry slot and red-orange dry-air comma wraps around the Southeast Pacific and southern South America, with another frontal band curving across the southwestern Atlantic east of southern Brazil and Uruguay. Both mark active mid-latitude troughs, and the orange-red streaks on their cyclonic sides are the better candidates in this image for stratospheric-intrusion-style dry air.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This CPC outlook for November 14-18, 2026 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the western and central U.S. The highest probabilities sit over the northern Plains and upper Midwest, with a core of 80-90% odds covering the Dakotas, Nebraska, Minnesota and adjacent parts of Montana, Wyoming and Iowa. Probabilities decline steadily toward the Pacific coast, where California and the coastal Northwest are only in the 33-40% "leaning above" categories, with a small near-normal pocket along the northern California coast.

In the East, the pattern flips. A band of near-normal extends from the Gulf Coast north through the Ohio Valley and Appalachians into the Northeast, and a below-normal area covers the Southeast Atlantic seaboard, strongest over Florida and southern Georgia (roughly 60-70%, the top category shown there) and weaker along the Carolinas and Virginia coast. A small above-normal area appears in northern Maine, and Alaska is mostly leaning above, with Hawaii also favored above.

Remember that these are probabilities of category, not temperature magnitudes, so the dark shading signals confidence rather than extreme departures. The geometry is a broad ridge-like warm signal centered over the Plains with cooler odds downstream in the Southeast. That is consistent with a western or central ridge and an eastern trough, though the chart itself does not show heights, so that is an inference. The tight east-west gradient from 80-90% above in the Plains to below-normal along the Atlantic coast implies a baroclinic zone that could host frontal passages along the Appalachians and Southeast.

On persistence versus breakdown, the outlook suggests the regime holds through mid-month, with the steepest gradient on the eastern flank of the warm anomaly. The usual caution applies: the lone strong cool signal is confined to Florida and the Southeast coast, so any eastward shift of the Plains warmth would first erode confidence in the Midwest and Ohio Valley, which are already transitioning toward near-normal.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook, valid Nov 14-18, 2026. Contours are labeled in meters (5160 to 5880 m, i.e. 516-588 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. The anomaly labels on the chart (90, 150, 210) are in meters, so they are a misleading-looking 9, 15 and 21 dam; I'm reading them as meters, and the exact labeling is partly obscured.

The dominant feature is a strong positive anomaly (red dashed) centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Hudson Bay, extending southward as a broad red corridor through central Canada into the Great Lakes and Northeast. Peak departures there are roughly 200 m (about 20 dam) above normal, with the 5400-5520 m contours bulging far north of their usual latitudes. A smaller positive center sits near the North Pole side of the domain, north of Greenland and Baffin Island. Negative anomalies (blue dashed) dominate the Pacific side: a deep center over the Bering Sea/western Alaska region, labeled near 5160 m, and a second broad negative zone off the Pacific Northwest and Gulf of Alaska, with departures of roughly 100-150 m (10-15 dam) below normal.

The implied pattern is a strongly amplified western trough and a ridge axis running from near the Arctic archipelago south through the Canadian Prairies, the Great Lakes, and the Northeast. The trough axis lies over the eastern Pacific, approaching the Pacific coast of North America, with the 5880 m contour pushed far northward across the central Pacific. The flow is meridional rather than zonal, with tightly packed height contours on both flanks of the ridge.

On the question of positive anomalies over western North America: they are essentially absent. The zero-anomaly line runs along or just inland of the Pacific coast, with negative departures covering British Columbia, the Pacific Northwest and much of the Intermountain West. The positive anomalies are displaced well to the north and east, centered over Hudson Bay and eastern Canada. This chart is a single time-mean outlook, so it cannot show trend by itself, but relative to a western ridge pattern, the ridge here sits much farther east and north, and zonal flow is not the signal.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook, made 8 Nov 2026 and valid Nov 16-22. One labeling note: the contours are annotated in meters (5340 through 5820, i.e. 534-582 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are also in meters at 60 m intervals, so the labels read 30, 60, 120, 150. In decameters that is roughly 3, 6, 12 and 15 dam.

The dominant feature is a broad positive anomaly (red dashed) centered over the central and eastern United States and south-central Canada, with the closed maxima spanning roughly the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley and western Hudson Bay region and peaking near the 150 m (about 15 dam) label over the Great Lakes/Ontario area. A second positive center sits farther north near the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, where heights run near 5220 m (522 dam). The ridge axis runs north-northeast from the Plains toward Hudson Bay, so the ridge core is over the eastern half of the continent, not the northern Rockies.

Over western Canada, the northern Rockies and the northern Plains the anomaly is not clearly positive: the purple zero line and blue negative contours (60 m, about 6 dam) sit along the Pacific Northwest and western Canada coast, and the western edge of the red positives lies near the Plains. The ridge has not retreated to the Southwest or northern Mexico either; the 5820 m contour runs across the southern tier, but the anomaly maxima remain well north and east of there.

A negative anomaly trough is evident near the West Coast and Gulf of Alaska, with a closed blue contour in the Gulf of Alaska region, and another weaker negative center over Greenland and the northwestern Atlantic (about -60 to -120 m, i.e. -6 to -12 dam). A mean trough lies over the western U.S. with strong zonal-to-southwesterly flow ahead of the eastern ridge, implying a mild pattern for much of the central and eastern U.S. in this ensemble-mean picture.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: This Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Monday 9 November through 12Z Tuesday 10 November 2026, shows only two categories: a green Marginal (at least 5%) area and a smaller Slight (at least 15%) area embedded within it. The Marginal area covers the lower Rio Grande valley and the southern Texas coastal plain, extending inland along the Texas–Mexico border and including adjacent northeastern Mexico, with its eastern edge near the Texas Gulf coast. The Slight risk, drawn in yellow and labeled SLGT, is a narrow north-south sliver near the lower Texas coast, apparently near the Rio Grande delta and the adjacent Mexican side. No Moderate or High risk is drawn, so Slight is the highest category on the chart. The rest of the contiguous United States carries no excessive-rainfall risk. The chart shows only risk categories, so it cannot say what is driving the rainfall. The compact, coast-hugging shape is consistent with a Gulf moisture surge or a nearby boundary rather than a broad frontal band, but the outlook itself does not show a tropical system, front or terrain forcing.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Tuesday November 10 through 12Z Wednesday November 11, 2026, draws no risk areas anywhere. The chart is blank across the contiguous United States, with a text box in the central Plains stating that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent. None of the legend categories (Marginal, Slight, Moderate, High) appear as shaded areas, so the lowest tier is not even in play for this period. The absence of any outline means the forecaster saw no region where even a Marginal-level threat (at least 5 percent) was warranted. A comparison with a Day 1 outlook cannot be made from this chart alone, since no Day 1 product is shown and there is no drawn risk to track as growing, shifting or relaxing. It is worth remembering that this product only addresses flash-flood-scale excessive rainfall, so it does not rule out ordinary rain or snow across the country, only the narrow category of rates and totals exceeding local flash flood guidance.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 259 AM EST Monday, November 9, 2026 (valid through 12Z Wednesday, November 11), the WPC forecast highlights:

Southern Texas faces a flash flood threat today. An upper-level low drawing Gulf moisture will bring scattered to widespread thunderstorms with locally very heavy downpours. WPC has a Slight Risk (level 2 of 4) of excessive rainfall for eastern South Texas, with activity diminishing by evening.

Pacific storm systems will bring moderate rain and higher-elevation snow to the Pacific Northwest, heaviest late Monday into Monday night.

Quick-moving lows will bring two rounds of scattered showers to the lower Great Lakes and Interior Northeast, today and again Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. Elsewhere, it should be mostly dry.

A chilly night is expected in the Tennessee Valleys and Southeast after frost advisories this morning. Otherwise, a warming trend spreads across much of the country. Highs will be in the 50s and 60s across the northern tier, 60s and 70s across the southern tier, and 80s in southern California, the Desert Southwest, and Florida. Cool, wet conditions will keep highs in the 50s and 60s over southern Texas and the Four Corners through Tuesday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook, issued 0640 AM CST Monday, November 9, 2026, valid 1300Z Nov 9 to 1200Z Nov 10. No severe thunderstorm areas are forecast, and organized severe thunderstorms are not expected through tonight.

South Texas: Elevated thunderstorms are ongoing this morning north of a weak inverted surface trough, supported by large-scale ascent and modest low-level warm advection ahead of a weak upper trough over west Texas and northern Mexico. Weak MUCAPE and poor lapse rates limit the severe threat. Any stronger storms should focus offshore through early afternoon.

Pacific Northwest: A fast-moving upper trough will cross the region this afternoon through tonight. Surface dewpoints in the upper 40s to low 50s and filtered heating may produce 100-300 J/kg MUCAPE ahead of a low-topped convective band moving quickly east across coastal Washington and Oregon. Occasional lightning is possible given cold mid-level temperatures. Strong low- and mid-level winds are conditionally favorable for organized updrafts, but meager instability should limit the severe gust risk.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours. The Storm Prediction Center is not actively monitoring any organized convective threat through this product at this time. This reflects the absence of mesoscale discussions only. It does not rule out severe weather, and other SPC products, such as watches and convective outlooks, should be checked for current conditions.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 7 AM EST Monday, November 9, 2026, the National Hurricane Center expects no tropical cyclone formation in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America through the next 7 days.

As of 4 AM PST Monday, November 9, 2026, the eastern and central North Pacific (east of 180 degrees longitude) has one active system. Tropical Storm Pena is several hundred miles south-southwest of the Big Island of Hawaii, and the Center is issuing advisories on it.

Elsewhere in the eastern Pacific, disturbance EP96 lies several hundred miles offshore of El Salvador and Nicaragua. Shower and thunderstorm activity has weakened. Conditions are expected to remain unfavorable as the system drifts west or west-southwest away from land. Chances of it becoming a short-lived tropical cyclone are decreasing. Formation odds are 10 percent through 48 hours and 10 percent through 7 days, both rated low.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
Product: NHC Active Storm Advisories, Tropical Storm Pena, as of 2026-11-09 09:00 UTC (11:00 PM HST Nov 8).

Pena is a tropical storm located near 11.3N, 158.4W, about 830 miles ESE of Johnston Island and 560 miles SSW of South Point, Hawaii. It is moving west (270 degrees) at 9 mph. Maximum sustained winds are about 40 kt (45 mph, 75 km/h) with higher gusts, and the minimum central pressure is 1002 mb. Tropical-storm-force winds extend up to 45 miles from the center.

No coastal watches or warnings are in effect, and no hazards are forecast to affect land.

Intensity: Light to moderate southerly vertical wind shear and drier mid-level air have kept Pena from strengthening, and little change is forecast over 48 hours. Shear is expected to ease in 12 to 24 hours, but only a few intensity models show modest strengthening. Toward the end of the period, shear from the west-southwest and dry air should cause weakening. Max winds are forecast to reach 45 kt around 36 to 72 hours, then fall back to 40 kt by 96 hours.

Track: Westward motion is expected for 48 to 60 hours, then a gradual turn toward the west-northwest around day 3, with forward speed increasing around day 3 to 4. Track guidance agrees well for the next couple of days, but spread increases later. Some regional hurricane models keep a more westward track, while the GFS, ECMWF, and consensus aids favor the west-northwest turn. The NHC track is close to the HCCA consensus.

Forecast positions: 48 h, 11.0N 166.6W; 72 h, 11.4N 171.8W; 96 h, 12.8N 178.4W; 120 h, 14.3N 177.1E.

Next complete advisory: 5:00 AM HST.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary:
The Oceanic Niño Index shows El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific, and they are strengthening. The index moved from -0.21 in JFM 2026, a cool-neutral reading, to positive values from April-May-June onward, with a steady rise each season.

The latest value, for August-September-October 2026, is +2.46°C, a strong El Niño by the usual threshold of +1.5°C or greater. Month-to-month increases have been slowing: the gain from JAS to ASO (+0.30) was smaller than the gains from MAM to MJJ (+0.93).

The table's absolute "TOTAL" column, the 3-month average sea surface temperature, rose from 26.57 to 29.23 over the same period. The product gives no issue date, so the currency of this latest season cannot be confirmed from the table alone.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices from NOAA CPC are stale. The newest value for all three is dated 2026-10-31, nine days before the product's current date, and CPC has not updated the table. Treat these as past observations, not current conditions.

As of 2026-10-31:

- PNA: +0.57, a rebound from -0.58 a few days earlier. The 7-day mean (-0.24) is below the prior week's (+0.06), so the index was falling over the period. A positive value favors western North American ridging with eastern troughing.
- AO: +0.77, positive. The 7-day mean (+1.03) is down from +1.44, so the positive phase was weakening. Positive values argue against high-latitude blocking.
- NAO: +1.15, positive. The 7-day mean (+0.59) is up from +0.26, so the index was rising. A positive NAO argues against an eastern cutoff escaping.

These extratropical indices are weaker outside winter, so use them only as directional support.
